entities.name: Octopus
entities.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood, and about two-thirds of its neurons sit in its eight arms rather than its brain.

entities.name: Squid
entities.fact: Squid swim by jet propulsion, squirting water from a flexible funnel, and some species can launch themselves clear of the surface.

entities.name: Cuttlefish
entities.fact: Cuttlefish control their buoyancy with a porous internal shell, the cuttlebone, and can change colour and skin texture in a fraction of a second.

entities.name: Nautilus
entities.fact: A nautilus has up to about 90 tentacles with no suckers, and its lineage of shelled cephalopods goes back about 500 million years.

entities.name: Chambered nautilus
entities.fact: The chambered nautilus adds new chambers to its spiral shell as it grows and adjusts the gas inside them to rise and sink.

entities.name: Crusty nautilus
entities.fact: The crusty nautilus of Papua New Guinea has a shell coated in a hairy, slimy layer and was not seen alive for about 30 years until 2015.

entities.name: Giant squid
entities.fact: The giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, about the size of a dinner plate, and was not filmed alive in the deep until 2012.

entities.name: Colossal squid
entities.fact: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is the heaviest invertebrate on Earth, reaching about 500 kilograms, with swivelling hooks on its tentacles.

entities.name: Humboldt squid
entities.fact: Humboldt squid hunt in packs of hundreds and flash red and white across their skin, earning the nickname 'red devil' from fishermen.

entities.name: Vampire squid
entities.fact: The vampire squid lives in oxygen-poor water around 600 to 900 metres down and, instead of ink, squirts a cloud of glowing mucus at threats.

entities.name: Firefly squid
entities.fact: Every spring millions of firefly squid rise to the surface of Toyama Bay in Japan, lighting the water blue with thousands of tiny photophores.

entities.name: Bobtail squid
entities.fact: Bobtail squid are small, round cephalopods that bury themselves in sand by day and hunt shrimp at night, and many carry glowing bacteria.

entities.name: Hawaiian bobtail squid
entities.fact: The Hawaiian bobtail squid houses glowing Vibrio bacteria in a light organ and uses them to erase its own shadow on moonlit nights.

entities.name: Glass squid
entities.fact: Glass squid are almost completely transparent and keep their one opaque organ, the digestive gland, pointed vertically so it casts the smallest shadow.

entities.name: Piglet squid
entities.fact: The piglet squid is a see-through, balloon-shaped deep-sea squid whose tuft of arms above a snout-like funnel gives it a comical piggy face.

entities.name: Caribbean reef squid
entities.fact: Caribbean reef squid talk with rapidly shifting skin patterns and can show one display to a mate and another to a rival at the same time.

entities.name: California market squid
entities.fact: The California market squid lives less than a year, spawns once in huge mass gatherings and supports one of California's most valuable fisheries.

entities.name: European squid
entities.fact: The European squid, the classic calamari of Mediterranean menus, has a body about 30 to 40 centimetres long and hunts fish in coastal waters.

entities.name: Veined squid
entities.fact: The veined squid is the main squid caught around Britain and Ireland, and can hover in place and change colour in an instant.

entities.name: Japanese flying squid
entities.fact: The Japanese flying squid supports one of the biggest squid fisheries in the world and can glide briefly above the waves by jetting water.

entities.name: Neon flying squid
entities.fact: Neon flying squid have been photographed gliding about 30 metres through the air, spreading their fins and arms like wings.

entities.name: Argentine shortfin squid
entities.fact: Hundreds of jigging boats light up the night off Argentina to catch this squid, one of the most heavily fished squid species on Earth.

entities.name: European flying squid
entities.fact: The European flying squid ranges from the Arctic to West Africa, and in some years swarms into Norwegian fjords in vast numbers.

entities.name: Bigfin reef squid
entities.fact: Bigfin reef squid have one of the fastest growth rates of any large invertebrate, reaching well over half a kilogram within about four months.

entities.name: Longfin inshore squid
entities.fact: The longfin inshore squid of the US Atlantic coast is a workhorse of neuroscience: its giant nerve fibre helped reveal how nerves fire.

entities.name: Strawberry squid
entities.fact: The strawberry squid has one big eye that looks up for shadows and one small eye that looks down for flashes of light, and skin dotted with photophores.

entities.name: Dana octopus squid
entities.fact: The Dana octopus squid carries the largest light organs in the animal kingdom, lemon-sized photophores on two of its arms that it flashes to stun prey.

entities.name: Ram's horn squid
entities.fact: The thumb-sized ram's horn squid keeps a coiled, chambered shell inside its body and carries a light organ on its rear end that it points upward.

entities.name: Diamond squid
entities.fact: The diamond squid swims in lifelong pairs and gets its name from the rhombus shape of fins that run the full length of its body.

entities.name: Giant warty squid
entities.fact: The giant warty squid of Antarctic waters can reach more than 2 metres in total length and is a major food of sperm whales and toothfish.

entities.name: Clawed armhook squid
entities.fact: The clawed armhook squid was the first squid seen brooding its eggs, carrying a sac of thousands of eggs in its arms for months in the deep.

entities.name: Pygmy squid
entities.fact: Pygmy squid are among the smallest cephalopods, about the size of a fingernail, and glue themselves to seagrass blades with a sticky patch on their back.

entities.name: Chokka squid
entities.fact: Chokka squid gather in huge spawning swarms off South Africa's southern coast, where they are hand-jigged for export as calamari.

entities.name: Whip-lash squid
entities.fact: Whip-lash squid hover over the deep seabed and trail two long, sticky tentacles covered in tiny suckers to catch small prey.

entities.name: Odd bobtail squid
entities.fact: The odd bobtail squid defends itself by squirting a glowing cloud of luminous mucus instead of dark ink.

entities.name: Bigfin squid
entities.fact: Bigfin squid dangle ten thin, elbowed arms that stretch to a total length of about 8 metres, and one was filmed 6,212 metres down in the Philippine Trench.

entities.name: Argonaut
entities.fact: The argonaut is really an octopus: the female secretes a paper-thin spiral shell as an egg case and uses it to trap air for buoyancy.

entities.name: Common octopus
entities.fact: The common octopus can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak and is a famous escape artist in aquariums and research labs.

entities.name: Giant Pacific octopus
entities.fact: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest octopus, with an arm span that can exceed 4 metres, and a female guards her eggs without eating until she dies.

entities.name: Blue-ringed octopus
entities.fact: A golf-ball-sized blue-ringed octopus carries enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, and its blue rings flash as a warning when it is alarmed.

entities.name: Greater blue-ringed octopus
entities.fact: Despite its name the greater blue-ringed octopus is only about 10 centimetres across; it is the size of its rings that is greater than its relatives'.

entities.name: Southern blue-ringed octopus
entities.fact: The southern blue-ringed octopus lives in tide pools and shallow reefs of southern Australia and delivers its venom through a bite that is often painless.

entities.name: Dumbo octopus
entities.fact: Dumbo octopuses flap ear-like fins to swim and have been filmed nearly 7,000 metres down in the Java Trench, deeper than any other octopus.

entities.name: Mimic octopus
entities.fact: The mimic octopus of Indonesia impersonates lionfish, flatfish and sea snakes by changing its shape, colour and the way it moves.

entities.name: Coconut octopus
entities.fact: The coconut octopus carries coconut shells across the seabed to use as a portable shelter, one of the clearest examples of tool use in an invertebrate.

entities.name: Blanket octopus
entities.fact: A female blanket octopus can be 2 metres long while the male is barely 2 centimetres, and they rip stinging tentacles from Portuguese man o' war to use as weapons.

entities.name: Day octopus
entities.fact: The day octopus hunts on tropical reefs in daylight, changing colour and texture many times a minute as it crosses different backgrounds.

entities.name: California two-spot octopus
entities.fact: The California two-spot octopus has a false blue eye-spot under each real eye and was the first octopus to have its full genome sequenced.

entities.name: Caribbean reef octopus
entities.fact: The Caribbean reef octopus spreads its webbed arms like a parachute over coral heads to trap crabs and shrimp underneath.

entities.name: East Pacific red octopus
entities.fact: The East Pacific red octopus is the most common shallow-water octopus from Alaska to Baja California, though its body is only about 10 centimetres long.

entities.name: Curled octopus
entities.fact: The curled octopus, common around Britain, holds its arms curled upward at the tips and has just a single row of suckers on each arm.

entities.name: Flapjack octopus
entities.fact: The flapjack octopus, a deep-sea dumbo relative that inspired Pearl in Finding Nemo, can flatten its webbed body into a pancake shape.

entities.name: Wunderpus
entities.fact: The wunderpus of Indonesian sand flats has a pattern of white bands so individual that scientists can identify each animal by its markings.

entities.name: Seven-arm octopus
entities.fact: The seven-arm octopus is one of the largest octopuses, with a 4-metre specimen known, and has been photographed holding and eating jellyfish.

entities.name: Glass octopus
entities.fact: The glass octopus is almost completely transparent; only its eyes, optic nerves and digestive tract show as it drifts through the open ocean.

entities.name: Gloomy octopus
entities.fact: Gloomy octopuses off eastern Australia gather at sites nicknamed Octopolis and Octlantis, where they have been filmed throwing shells and silt at each other.

entities.name: Atlantic pygmy octopus
entities.fact: The Atlantic pygmy octopus is small enough to live inside an empty clam shell, which it pulls shut around itself with its suckers.

entities.name: Algae octopus
entities.fact: The algae octopus disguises itself as a shell overgrown with weed and can walk away on two arms while holding the other six in a ball.

entities.name: Giant Antarctic octopus
entities.fact: The giant Antarctic octopus, the largest octopus in the Southern Ocean, has venom that keeps working at freezing temperatures.

entities.name: Star-sucker pygmy octopus
entities.fact: The star-sucker pygmy octopus is the smallest known octopus, about 2.5 centimetres long and weighing less than a gram.

entities.name: Larger Pacific striped octopus
entities.fact: The larger Pacific striped octopus is unusually social: pairs share dens and mate beak to beak, and the female lays several clutches instead of dying after one.

entities.name: Telescope octopus
entities.fact: The telescope octopus is a see-through deep-sea octopus with tubular eyes on stalks that point upward to spot prey against the faint light.

entities.name: Football octopus
entities.fact: The football octopus is the only cephalopod with a true swim bladder, and its tiny males ride inside empty salp barrels in the open ocean.

entities.name: Musky octopus
entities.fact: The musky octopus of the Mediterranean gives off a distinct musky smell and has a single row of suckers on each arm.

entities.name: White-spotted octopus
entities.fact: The white-spotted octopus hunts at night, flushing bright red with white spots and reaching its long arms deep into coral crevices.

entities.name: Patagonian red octopus
entities.fact: The Patagonian red octopus is fished along the coasts of Chile and Argentina and is a close relative of the giant Pacific octopus.

entities.name: Casper octopus
entities.fact: A ghost-white octopus nicknamed Casper was discovered off Hawaii in 2016 at about 4,000 metres, laying its eggs on dead sponge stalks attached to metal nodules.

entities.name: Glowing sucker octopus
entities.fact: The glowing sucker octopus has suckers that no longer grip but glow blue-green, probably to lure the tiny copepods it eats.

entities.name: Vent octopus
entities.fact: The vent octopus is a small, pale, nearly blind octopus found only around hydrothermal vents on the East Pacific Rise.

entities.name: Common cuttlefish
entities.fact: The common cuttlefish has W-shaped pupils and can send rippling waves of colour across its skin even though it is thought to be colour-blind.

entities.name: Flamboyant cuttlefish
entities.fact: The flamboyant cuttlefish walks along the seabed on its arms and is the only cuttlefish known to have poisonous flesh.

entities.name: Giant cuttlefish
entities.fact: Australian giant cuttlefish gather in their tens of thousands each winter to breed at Whyalla, where small males disguise themselves as females to sneak past rivals.

entities.name: Broadclub cuttlefish
entities.fact: The broadclub cuttlefish hypnotises crabs by flashing moving bands of dark colour down its arms before striking.

entities.name: Pharaoh cuttlefish
entities.fact: The pharaoh cuttlefish of the Indo-Pacific is one of the most heavily fished cuttlefish and is also bred in labs for research.

entities.name: Dwarf cuttlefish
entities.fact: The dwarf cuttlefish grows to only about 7 centimetres and is a favourite in research labs and home aquariums for its rapid colour changes.

entities.name: Crab
entities.fact: Crabs walk sideways because of the way their leg joints bend, and a crab can regrow a lost claw at its next moult.

entities.name: Hermit crab
entities.fact: Hermit crabs have a soft, curled abdomen and move into bigger empty snail shells as they grow, sometimes queueing up to swap shells in order of size.

entities.name: King crab
entities.fact: King crabs are not true crabs but giant relatives of hermit crabs, with three visible pairs of walking legs instead of four.

entities.name: Red king crab
entities.fact: The red king crab can span 1.8 metres leg to leg and has invaded the Barents Sea since Soviet scientists introduced it there in the 1960s.

entities.name: Blue crab
entities.fact: The blue crab's scientific name means 'beautiful savoury swimmer', and freshly moulted ones are eaten whole as soft-shell crabs.

entities.name: Fiddler crab
entities.fact: A male fiddler crab has one claw far bigger than the other and waves it to attract females and warn off rivals.

entities.name: Japanese spider crab
entities.fact: The Japanese spider crab has the largest leg span of any arthropod, up to about 3.7 metres, and lives on the seabed off Japan down to about 600 metres.

entities.name: Coconut crab
entities.fact: The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod, climbs trees and cracks coconuts with claws that pinch harder than almost any animal bites.

entities.name: Snow crab
entities.fact: Billions of snow crabs vanished from the Bering Sea after a marine heatwave, closing Alaska's snow crab fishery for the first time in 2022.

entities.name: Dungeness crab
entities.fact: The Dungeness crab, named after a small town in Washington State, is one of the most valuable fisheries on the US West Coast.

entities.name: Stone crab
entities.fact: Florida stone crabs are fished for their claws alone: a claw is removed and the live crab is returned to the sea to grow a new one.

entities.name: Ghost crab
entities.fact: Ghost crabs are pale beach crabs that dig deep burrows and are among the fastest crustaceans on land, sprinting at more than 2 metres per second.

entities.name: Shore crab
entities.fact: The shore crab, the common rock-pool crab of Europe, has spread around the world in ships' ballast water and is one of the most invasive marine species.

entities.name: Edible crab
entities.fact: The edible or brown crab, with its pie-crust shell edge, is the most heavily fished crab in Western Europe.

entities.name: Spider crab
entities.fact: European spider crabs pile up in mounds of hundreds during their summer moult and decorate their spiny shells with seaweed.

entities.name: Mud crab
entities.fact: The giant mud crab of mangrove estuaries has claws strong enough to crack a mussel shell or a careless finger, and is the crab in Singapore chilli crab.

entities.name: Chinese mitten crab
entities.fact: The Chinese mitten crab has furry claws, lives in rivers but breeds in the sea, and has invaded the Thames, the Elbe and San Francisco Bay.

entities.name: Yeti crab
entities.fact: The yeti crab, discovered in 2005 at vents south of Easter Island, has hairy arms coated in bacteria that it is thought to feed on.

entities.name: Porcelain crab
entities.fact: Porcelain crabs are flat, fragile crab-like animals that filter plankton with feathery mouthparts and readily drop a leg to escape.

entities.name: Sally Lightfoot crab
entities.fact: Sally Lightfoot crabs skitter over Galápagos lava rocks in bright red and blue, and pick ticks off basking marine iguanas.

entities.name: Velvet crab
entities.fact: The velvet crab of European shores has red eyes, a furry shell and a famously aggressive temper, and is caught for Spanish markets.

entities.name: Pea crab
entities.fact: The pea crab is a tiny crab that lives inside the shells of living mussels and oysters, stealing food from its host's gills.

entities.name: Decorator crab
entities.fact: Decorator crabs snip bits of sponge, seaweed and anemone and hook them onto bristles on their shell as living camouflage.

entities.name: Christmas Island red crab
entities.fact: Tens of millions of Christmas Island red crabs march from the forest to the sea each year to breed, closing roads across the island.

entities.name: Tasmanian giant crab
entities.fact: The Tasmanian giant crab can weigh more than 13 kilograms and has one huge claw; it lives on the edge of the continental shelf off southern Australia.

entities.name: Arrow crab
entities.fact: The arrow crab of Caribbean reefs has spindly legs and a pointed head, and is kept in aquariums to eat bristle worms.

entities.name: Jonah crab
entities.fact: The Jonah crab of the north-west Atlantic was once lobster-pot bycatch but is now fished in its own right for its large claws.

entities.name: Horsehair crab
entities.fact: The horsehair crab of Hokkaido is covered in short bristles and is prized in Japan for its sweet meat and rich crab liver.

entities.name: Spanner crab
entities.fact: The spanner crab walks forwards instead of sideways and has flattened claws shaped like spanners, used to dig into sand.

entities.name: Masked crab
entities.fact: The masked crab buries itself in sand and breathes through a snorkel made of its two long antennae pressed together.

entities.name: Sand bubbler crab
entities.fact: Sand bubbler crabs sift sand for food and leave thousands of tiny sand balls radiating from their burrows on tropical beaches at low tide.

entities.name: Columbus crab
entities.fact: The Columbus crab lives on floating sargassum and on the backs of loggerhead turtles, hitching rides across the open Atlantic.

entities.name: Sponge crab
entities.fact: Sponge crabs cut a living sponge to size and hold it over their backs with their hind legs as a hat that grows with them.

entities.name: Pom-pom crab
entities.fact: The pom-pom crab holds a live sea anemone in each claw and waves them like boxing gloves; if it loses one it tears the other in half to grow a new pair.

entities.name: Vent crab
entities.fact: Bythograea vent crabs are the top scavengers and predators of East Pacific vent fields, picking over tube worms, mussels and dead fish.

entities.name: Hoff crab
entities.fact: The Hoff crab, named for its hairy chest after actor David Hasselhoff, crowds by the thousand onto hot vent chimneys on the Antarctic East Scotia Ridge.

entities.name: Lobster
entities.fact: Lobsters keep growing throughout their lives, moulting their shell to get bigger, and some are thought to live for more than 50 years.

entities.name: American lobster
entities.fact: The American lobster is the heaviest crustacean ever recorded, with a 20-kilogram giant caught off Nova Scotia in 1977.

entities.name: European lobster
entities.fact: The European lobster is dark blue when alive and only turns red when it is cooked, as heat breaks down the pigment that masks the red.

entities.name: Spiny lobster
entities.fact: Spiny lobsters have no big claws but long spiny antennae, and march across the seabed in single-file queues of dozens before winter storms.

entities.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
entities.fact: The Caribbean spiny lobster can navigate home using the Earth's magnetic field, the first invertebrate shown to have a magnetic map sense.

entities.name: Slipper lobster
entities.fact: Slipper lobsters have flat, plate-like antennae instead of long feelers and are sold in Australia as Moreton Bay bugs and Balmain bugs.

entities.name: Japanese spiny lobster
entities.fact: The Japanese spiny lobster, Ise-ebi, is a celebration food in Japan, served grilled or raw at New Year and at weddings.

entities.name: Squat lobster
entities.fact: Squat lobsters are flattened crab-like relatives of hermit crabs that tuck their tails under their bodies and swarm on deep-sea coral and vent fields.

entities.name: Vent squat lobster
entities.fact: Munidopsis squat lobsters, pale and nearly blind, crawl in crowds around the cooler fringes of vent fields, scavenging whatever drifts their way.

entities.name: Langoustine
entities.fact: Langoustines live in burrows in muddy seabeds and are one of the most valuable catches landed in Britain, where they are sold as scampi.

entities.name: Crayfish
entities.fact: Crayfish are freshwater relatives of lobsters, and Louisiana alone boils up tens of thousands of tonnes of them every year.

entities.name: Signal crayfish
entities.fact: The signal crayfish, named for the white patch at its claw joints, was introduced from North America and now dominates rivers across Europe.

entities.name: Red swamp crayfish
entities.fact: The red swamp crayfish is the star of Louisiana crawfish boils and has spread as an invader to rivers and rice paddies across Europe, Africa and Asia.

entities.name: White-clawed crayfish
entities.fact: The white-clawed crayfish, Britain's only native crayfish, is being wiped out by a fungal plague carried by invasive American signal crayfish.

entities.name: Marron
entities.fact: The marron of Western Australia is one of the largest freshwater crayfish, reaching more than 2 kilograms, and is farmed for restaurants.

entities.name: Yabby
entities.fact: The yabby of Australian creeks and farm dams digs so deep into mud to survive drought that its scientific name means 'destroyer'.

entities.name: Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish
entities.fact: The Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish is the largest freshwater invertebrate on Earth, once reaching about 6 kilograms, and can live for about 40 years.

entities.name: Shrimp
entities.fact: Shrimps range from tide pools to trench floors: decapod shrimps have been filmed in the Kermadec Trench more than 7,000 metres down.

entities.name: Prawn
entities.fact: Prawn and shrimp are not scientific terms: Britain and Australia mostly say prawn and North America mostly says shrimp for the same animals.

entities.name: Tiger prawn
entities.fact: The giant tiger prawn grows to about 33 centimetres, one of the largest prawns, and has escaped from farms to invade the Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Whiteleg shrimp
entities.fact: The whiteleg shrimp is the most farmed shrimp in the world, raised in ponds from Ecuador to Vietnam and sold by the million as supermarket prawns.

entities.name: Mantis shrimp
entities.fact: A mantis shrimp strikes with the acceleration of a bullet and sees with up to 16 types of light-sensing cell, compared with our three.

entities.name: Peacock mantis shrimp
entities.fact: The peacock mantis shrimp's club-like arms hit so hard they can crack aquarium glass and shatter crab shells in a single blow.

entities.name: Pistol shrimp
entities.fact: A pistol shrimp snaps its claw shut so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that briefly approaches the temperature of the Sun's surface and stuns prey.

entities.name: Cleaner shrimp
entities.fact: Cleaner shrimp wave their white antennae to advertise a cleaning service, and reef fish queue up and open their mouths to have parasites picked off.

entities.name: Northern prawn
entities.fact: The northern prawn starts life as a male and changes into a female after a few years, and is the cold-water prawn in most prawn cocktails.

entities.name: Brown shrimp
entities.fact: The brown shrimp of the North Sea is caught by horseback shrimpers in Belgium and potted in butter around Morecambe Bay.

entities.name: Harlequin shrimp
entities.fact: Harlequin shrimp hunt in pairs and eat only starfish, flipping their prey over and feeding on it alive for days.

entities.name: Peppermint shrimp
entities.fact: The peppermint shrimp is stocked in reef aquariums because it eats the pest anemone Aiptasia.

entities.name: Spot prawn
entities.fact: The spot prawn is the largest shrimp on the North American Pacific coast and is eaten raw as amaebi in sushi bars.

entities.name: Banded coral shrimp
entities.fact: The banded coral shrimp waves long white antennae from reef crevices to attract fish, which it then cleans of parasites.

entities.name: Common prawn
entities.fact: The common prawn of European rock pools is almost transparent with faint stripes, and is netted along British and Irish coasts for the table.

entities.name: Kuruma prawn
entities.fact: The kuruma prawn, with its banded tail, is one of the most expensive prawns in Japan and the first prawn ever reared in a hatchery, in the 1930s.

entities.name: Emperor shrimp
entities.fact: The emperor shrimp rides on sea cucumbers and Spanish dancer nudibranchs, picking food from the sand as its host crawls along.

entities.name: Sexy shrimp
entities.fact: The sexy shrimp got its name from the way it constantly sways its tail up and down while sitting on a sea anemone.

entities.name: Akiami paste shrimp
entities.fact: The thumbnail-sized Akiami paste shrimp is caught in bigger tonnages than any other shrimp species, mostly for shrimp paste and dried shrimp in Asia.

entities.name: Vent shrimp
entities.fact: Rimicaris vent shrimp swarm in thousands on Mid-Atlantic vent chimneys and have no normal eyes, only a light-sensing patch on the back that detects the vents' faint glow.

entities.name: Alvinocaris shrimp
entities.fact: Alvinocaris shrimp were among the first animals described from the Galápagos Rift vents after their discovery in 1977, scavenging among tube worms and clams.

entities.name: Acanthephyra shrimp
entities.fact: Deep-sea Acanthephyra shrimp are blood-red, which looks black in the depths, and spit a cloud of glowing blue liquid into a predator's face.

entities.name: Benthesicymus
entities.fact: The prawn Benthesicymus crenatus was filmed in the Kermadec and Japan trenches at about 7,700 metres, the first decapod seen in the hadal zone.

entities.name: Opossum shrimp
entities.fact: Opossum shrimp carry their young in a pouch like a possum and swarm in glassy clouds in caves, estuaries and the deep sea.

entities.name: Pederson's cleaner shrimp
entities.fact: Pederson's cleaner shrimp is see-through with violet spots and lives on Caribbean anemones, where it cleans parasites from visiting fish.

entities.name: Anemone shrimp
entities.fact: The glass anemone shrimp is transparent apart from a few white and orange spots, and lives unharmed among the stinging tentacles of its host anemone.

entities.name: Krill
entities.fact: Antarctic krill swarms can stretch for kilometres, and their total weight of several hundred million tonnes is among the largest of any animal species.

entities.name: Amphipod
entities.fact: Scavenging amphipods swarm onto any bait lowered to the floor of the Mariana Trench within minutes, even at the very bottom of the Challenger Deep.

entities.name: Hirondellea gigas
entities.fact: Hirondellea gigas amphipods swarm at the bottom of the Challenger Deep and make enzymes that digest sunken wood and plant debris.

entities.name: Supergiant amphipod
entities.fact: The supergiant amphipod grows to about 34 centimetres, around ten times the size of most amphipods, and was caught 7,000 metres down in the Kermadec Trench.

entities.name: Eurythenes plasticus
entities.fact: This amphipod from nearly 7,000 metres down in the Mariana Trench was named 'plasticus' in 2020 because microplastic fibres were found in its gut.

entities.name: Vent amphipod
entities.fact: Ventiella amphipods swarm in dense clouds around East Pacific vents, feeding on bacterial mats and dead tube worms.

entities.name: Giant isopod
entities.fact: The giant isopod is a deep-sea relative of the woodlouse that grows to about 40 centimetres and can go for years without a meal.

entities.name: Isopod
entities.fact: Isopods, the group that includes woodlice, are found in every ocean habitat, including trench floors deeper than 6,000 metres.

entities.name: Tanaid
entities.fact: Tanaids are tiny, shrimp-like crustaceans that build tubes in the mud and are among the commonest animals in deep trench sediments.

entities.name: Copepod
entities.fact: Copepods are the most numerous animals in the sea by a wide margin, and have been found in the mud at the bottom of the Challenger Deep.

entities.name: Vent copepod
entities.fact: Dirivultid copepods are found only at hydrothermal vents, where they are often the most numerous animals crawling over tube worms and mussels.

entities.name: Sea sapphire
entities.fact: The sea sapphire is a copepod whose males flash brilliant blue, then turn transparent and vanish as they tilt, thanks to crystal plates in their skin.

entities.name: Phronima
entities.fact: Phronima is a transparent amphipod that hollows out a salp and lives inside the barrel, rearing its young there as it drifts.

entities.name: Goose barnacle
entities.fact: Goose barnacles, percebes in Spain, are gathered from wave-battered rocks and are among the most expensive seafood in Europe; medieval writers thought geese hatched from them.

entities.name: Buoy barnacle
entities.fact: The buoy barnacle makes its own float, a foam of cement bubbles, and drifts across the open ocean hanging beneath it.

entities.name: Vent barnacle
entities.fact: Vent barnacles grow in dense clusters on vent chimneys, with long bristly feeding legs that host the bacteria they feed on.

entities.name: Sea firefly
entities.fact: The sea firefly is a 3-millimetre ostracod that squirts glowing blue mucus; dried ones were used by Japanese soldiers as a dim reading light.

entities.name: Oyster
entities.fact: A single oyster can filter about 190 litres of water a day, and oysters change sex, usually starting life as males.

entities.name: Mussel
entities.fact: Mussels anchor themselves to rocks with tough byssus threads, a natural glue so strong that engineers copy it for surgical adhesives.

entities.name: Clam
entities.fact: Clams are bivalves that dig with a muscular foot, and in the Japan Trench clams fed by bacteria live more than 7,000 metres down.

entities.name: Scallop
entities.fact: Scallops have up to about 200 tiny blue eyes along the edge of the shell and swim by clapping their two shells together.

entities.name: Cockle
entities.fact: Cockles live just under the surface of sandy shores and are raked up at low tide, famously on the sands of Morecambe Bay and the Gower.

entities.name: Abalone
entities.fact: Abalone are large sea snails with a row of breathing holes along the shell and iridescent mother-of-pearl inside, prized for food and jewellery.

entities.name: Ormer
entities.fact: The ormer is the European abalone, gathered by hand on Channel Island beaches at low tide on a handful of strictly controlled days each year.

entities.name: Conch
entities.fact: The queen conch is a big Caribbean sea snail that hops along on a claw-shaped foot and is eaten in fritters, salads and chowder.

entities.name: Whelk
entities.fact: The common whelk is a cold-water sea snail boiled and sold at British seaside stalls and exported to South Korea in large quantities.

entities.name: Periwinkle
entities.fact: Winkles are small sea snails picked from rocks at low tide and eaten with a pin to pull them from the shell.

entities.name: Limpet
entities.fact: Limpet teeth are made of the strongest biological material known, and each limpet returns to the same home scar on its rock after grazing.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck is a giant clam of the Pacific Northwest with a siphon up to a metre long, and can live for more than 150 years.

entities.name: Razor clam
entities.fact: Razor clams shoot down into wet sand faster than a person can dig, and are lured up by pouring salt into their keyhole-shaped burrows.

entities.name: Quahog
entities.fact: The quahog is the hard clam of New England chowder, and its cousin the ocean quahog, dredged off Iceland, lived to 507 years, the oldest animal ever aged.

entities.name: Soft-shell clam
entities.fact: Soft-shell clams, the 'steamers' of New England clam shacks, have a long neck that squirts water when you walk over the mud flat.

entities.name: Manila clam
entities.fact: The Manila clam is the most farmed clam in the world and reached North America by accident, mixed in with oyster seed shipped from Japan.

entities.name: European flat oyster
entities.fact: The European flat oyster was once so common that it was poor people's food in Victorian London; reefs of it are now being restored around Britain.

entities.name: Sydney rock oyster
entities.fact: The Sydney rock oyster has been farmed in New South Wales estuaries since the 1870s, making it Australia's oldest aquaculture industry.

entities.name: Green-lipped mussel
entities.fact: The green-lipped mussel is found only in New Zealand, where it is farmed on ropes and exported worldwide, including as a joint supplement.

entities.name: Pipi
entities.fact: Pipi are wedge-shaped surf clams dug from sandy beaches in Australia and New Zealand, traditionally found by twisting your feet into the wet sand.

entities.name: Scaly-foot snail
entities.fact: The scaly-foot snail armours its foot with plates of iron sulphide and is the first species declared endangered because of deep-sea mining.

entities.name: Hairy vent snail
entities.fact: Alviniconcha vent snails have bristly shells and gills packed with bacteria that feed them, so they barely need to eat.

entities.name: Ifremeria snail
entities.fact: Ifremeria snails cluster in dense beds at western Pacific vents and brood their young inside a pouch in the foot.

entities.name: Vent limpet
entities.fact: Tiny Lepetodrilus limpets carpet tube worms and mussels at vents by the thousand, grazing the bacterial film that coats everything.

entities.name: Blue dragon
entities.fact: The blue dragon sea slug floats upside down at the surface, eats Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its finger-like tips to fire at attackers.

entities.name: Violet sea snail
entities.fact: The violet sea snail cannot swim: it hangs upside down from a raft of mucus bubbles and drifts until it bumps into a by-the-wind sailor to eat.

entities.name: Cone snail
entities.fact: Cone snails fire a venom-filled harpoon tooth into fish, and one of their toxins has been turned into a painkiller stronger than morphine.

entities.name: Geography cone
entities.fact: The geography cone is the deadliest cone snail, nicknamed the cigarette snail because a stung person was said to have time for one cigarette before dying.

entities.name: Sea snail
entities.fact: Sea snails live at every depth in the ocean: tiny turrid snails have been found more than 10,000 metres down in trenches.

entities.name: Sea butterfly
entities.fact: Sea butterflies are tiny swimming snails with transparent shells and wing-like flaps, and their shells dissolve as seawater grows more acidic.

entities.name: Sea angel
entities.fact: The sea angel is a shell-less, translucent swimming snail that flaps two wings and shoots out hooked tentacles to drag sea butterflies from their shells.

entities.name: Jellyfish
entities.fact: Jellyfish have no brain, heart or blood and are more than 95 per cent water, yet they have drifted the oceans for more than 500 million years.

entities.name: Box jellyfish
entities.fact: The Australian box jellyfish has 24 eyes and a sting that can stop a human heart within minutes, and it is almost invisible in the water.

entities.name: Irukandji jellyfish
entities.fact: The Irukandji jellyfish is barely the size of a fingernail and transparent, yet its sting causes hours of agony, vomiting and a feeling of impending doom.

entities.name: Portuguese man o' war
entities.fact: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised animals under a gas-filled sail, trailing tentacles that can reach 30 metres.

entities.name: Moon jellyfish
entities.fact: The moon jellyfish is see-through with four horseshoe-shaped gonads visible through its bell, and its sting is too weak to hurt most people.

entities.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
entities.fact: The lion's mane is the largest jellyfish, with a bell up to about 2 metres across and tentacles that can trail more than 30 metres.

entities.name: Immortal jellyfish
entities.fact: The immortal jellyfish can turn its adult body back into a juvenile polyp when injured or starving, restarting its life cycle indefinitely.

entities.name: Comb jelly
entities.fact: Comb jellies are not true jellyfish: they swim with eight rows of beating cilia that scatter light into rainbows, and most species also glow blue in the dark.

entities.name: Sea nettle
entities.fact: Sea nettles are golden-brown jellyfish with long frilly oral arms whose sting feels like brushing a stinging nettle, hence the name.

entities.name: Cannonball jellyfish
entities.fact: The cannonball jellyfish is fished off Georgia and Florida, dried and exported to Asia as a crunchy salad ingredient.

entities.name: Upside-down jellyfish
entities.fact: The upside-down jellyfish lies on its back in mangrove shallows so the algae in its arms get sunlight, and releases stinging blobs of mucus into the water.

entities.name: Blue blubber jellyfish
entities.fact: The blue blubber of Australian estuaries has no trailing tentacles, feeding with eight stubby arms, and is fished and dried for export to Asia.

entities.name: Fried egg jellyfish
entities.fact: The fried egg jellyfish of the Mediterranean looks exactly like its name, with a yellow dome on a white bell, and small fish shelter among its arms.

entities.name: Nomura's jellyfish
entities.fact: Nomura's jellyfish can weigh 200 kilograms and measure 2 metres across, and swarms drifting from China into Japanese waters have capsized a fishing boat.

entities.name: Crystal jelly
entities.fact: The transparent crystal jelly is the source of green fluorescent protein, which won a Nobel Prize and now lights up cells in labs worldwide.

entities.name: By-the-wind sailor
entities.fact: The by-the-wind sailor floats on the surface under a stiff diagonal sail, so whole fleets of them are blown ashore in the same storm.

entities.name: Mauve stinger
entities.fact: The mauve stinger glows when disturbed at night and has caused mass stingings on Mediterranean beaches; one swarm wiped out a salmon farm in Northern Ireland.

entities.name: Barrel jellyfish
entities.fact: The barrel jellyfish, the largest jellyfish in British waters, can reach the size of a dustbin lid and is harmless enough to be food for leatherback turtles.

entities.name: Compass jellyfish
entities.fact: The compass jellyfish has brown V-shaped markings radiating across its bell like the points of a compass, and it starts life male and becomes female.

entities.name: Flower hat jelly
entities.fact: The flower hat jelly of Japan has fluorescent pink-tipped tentacles coiled around its rim and spends the day resting on the seabed.

entities.name: Crown jellyfish
entities.fact: The deep-sea crown jellyfish Atolla sets off a spinning blue 'burglar alarm' of light when attacked, calling in bigger predators to eat its attacker.

entities.name: Sea gooseberry
entities.fact: The sea gooseberry is a glassy, marble-sized comb jelly that trails two long sticky tentacles to snare copepods.

entities.name: Sea walnut
entities.fact: The sea walnut, a comb jelly from the American Atlantic, invaded the Black Sea in ballast water and helped collapse its anchovy fishery in the 1980s.

entities.name: Blue button
entities.fact: The blue button is a coin-sized floating colony of hydroids with a hard golden disc and a fringe of blue tentacles, often washed up with by-the-wind sailors.

entities.name: Spotted jelly
entities.fact: Millions of golden jellyfish follow the sun across Palau's Jellyfish Lake each day to feed the algae in their tissues, and their sting is too mild to notice.

entities.name: Bloodybelly comb jelly
entities.fact: The bloodybelly comb jelly is deep red so that the glowing prey in its stomach cannot be seen by predators in the dark depths.

entities.name: Venus girdle
entities.fact: The Venus girdle is a ribbon-shaped, transparent comb jelly up to about 1.5 metres long that ripples through the water like a strip of glass.

entities.name: Big red jellyfish
entities.fact: Big red is a metre-wide deep-sea jellyfish discovered in 2003 that has no tentacles at all, feeding instead with four to seven thick fleshy arms.

entities.name: Black sea nettle
entities.fact: The black sea nettle has a bell up to a metre across and oral arms about 8 metres long, yet it was not formally described until 1997.

entities.name: Helmet jellyfish
entities.fact: The helmet jellyfish lives in deep water and in dark Norwegian fjords, where it has multiplied so much that it has displaced the fish.

entities.name: Thimble jellyfish
entities.fact: The thumb-sized thimble jellyfish's larvae cause 'sea bather's eruption', an itchy rash under swimsuits along Florida and Caribbean beaches.

entities.name: Deepstaria
entities.fact: Deepstaria is a deep-sea jellyfish like a loose, bag-shaped sheet that closes around prey the way a drawstring sack does.

entities.name: Siphonophore
entities.fact: A siphonophore is a chain of specialised clones acting as one animal; one filmed off Western Australia in 2020 was estimated at about 45 metres long.

entities.name: Giant siphonophore
entities.fact: The giant siphonophore Praya dubia can reach 40 to 50 metres long, among the longest animals on Earth, and its stinging tentacles glow when touched.

entities.name: Dandelion siphonophore
entities.fact: The dandelion siphonophore tethers itself to rocks at Pacific vents with fine threads, looking like a dandelion seed head, and eats scraps from the vent community.

entities.name: Stalked jellyfish
entities.fact: Stalked jellyfish are tiny trumpet-shaped jellyfish that live upside down, glued by a stalk to seaweed and seagrass instead of swimming.

entities.name: Hydroid
entities.fact: Hydroids are plant-like colonies of stinging polyps, the attached stage of many jellyfish, and have been dredged from more than 8,200 metres in the Kermadec Trench.

entities.name: Sea anemone
entities.fact: Sea anemones look like flowers but are predators armed with stinging tentacles, found from rock pools to the floors of ocean trenches.

entities.name: Beadlet anemone
entities.fact: The beadlet anemone of British rock pools is a red blob at low tide, and fights its neighbours with a ring of blue stinging beads under its tentacles.

entities.name: Snakelocks anemone
entities.fact: The snakelocks anemone cannot fully pull in its long green tentacles, which get their colour from algae living inside them and their purple tips from a pigment.

entities.name: Plumose anemone
entities.fact: The plumose anemone is a tall white or orange anemone with a feathery crown of hundreds of fine tentacles, common on wrecks and pier legs.

entities.name: Tube anemone
entities.fact: Tube anemones live inside a slimy tube buried in sand and can withdraw their two rings of long tentacles in a flash when disturbed.

entities.name: Venus flytrap anemone
entities.fact: The deep-sea Venus flytrap anemone folds its tentacled disc shut around prey, like the plant it is named after.

entities.name: Vent anemone
entities.fact: Pale sea anemones fringe the cooler edges of hydrothermal vent fields, catching scraps carried past by the warm, murky water.

entities.name: Coral
entities.fact: Coral is built by tiny animals called polyps, each a ring of stinging tentacles around a mouth, which together lay down reefs visible from space.

entities.name: Fire coral
entities.fact: Fire coral is not a true coral but a relative of jellyfish, and brushing its yellow-brown branches leaves a burning sting.

entities.name: Sea pen
entities.fact: A sea pen is a colony of polyps shaped like an old quill pen, rooted in soft mud, and many species glow green when touched.

entities.name: Giant tube worm
entities.fact: The giant tube worm has no mouth or gut: bacteria inside it turn vent sulphide into food, letting it grow to 2 metres, nearly a metre of it in a single year.

entities.name: Pompeii worm
entities.fact: The Pompeii worm lives in tubes on vent chimneys with its tail in water of around 80 degrees Celsius, making it one of the most heat-tolerant animals known.

entities.name: Zombie worm
entities.fact: Zombie worms have no mouth or stomach; they bore roots into whale bones on the seabed and let bacteria digest the fat, and the dwarf males live inside the females.

entities.name: Jericho worm
entities.fact: The Jericho worm is a tube worm with a ringed tube like a crumbling wall, and it is usually the first tube worm to colonise a brand-new vent.

entities.name: Palm worm
entities.fact: The palm worm builds mucus tubes on Pacific vent chimneys and spreads a crown of tentacles like a palm tree to feed in the hot water.

entities.name: Sulphide worm
entities.fact: The sulphide worm chooses to sit in water of about 50 degrees Celsius on vent chimneys, hotter than any other animal has been shown to prefer.

entities.name: Ridgeia tube worm
entities.fact: Ridgeia tube worms blanket the vents of the Juan de Fuca Ridge off Canada, growing tall and thin or short and fat depending on how hot their spot is.

entities.name: Oasisia tube worm
entities.fact: Oasisia is a slender tube worm that grows in tangles among giant tube worms at East Pacific vents and, like them, feeds through bacteria instead of a mouth.

entities.name: Vent scale worm
entities.fact: Branchipolynoe scale worms live inside the shells of living vent mussels, with special blood that stores oxygen for when the vent water turns foul.

entities.name: Vent spaghetti worm
entities.fact: Vent spaghetti worms are acorn worms that drape themselves over rocks in tangled strands at the Galápagos Rift vents, mopping bacteria off the surface.

entities.name: Bristle worm
entities.fact: Bristle worms are segmented worms with paddle-like feet fringed with bristles, and they have been collected from the mud at the bottom of the Challenger Deep.

entities.name: Christmas tree worm
entities.fact: The Christmas tree worm lives in a tube bored into coral and unfurls two spiral crowns of tentacles that snap back inside in a blink.

entities.name: Feather duster worm
entities.fact: Feather duster worms spread a fan of feathery tentacles from a parchment tube to trap plankton, and many have eyes on the tentacles to spot shadows.

entities.name: Bermuda fireworm
entities.fact: Bermuda fireworms rise to the surface a few nights after each summer full moon and spin in glowing green circles to mate, a display Columbus may have seen in 1492.

entities.name: Tomopteris
entities.fact: Tomopteris is a transparent swimming worm of the open ocean and one of the very few animals able to make yellow light.

entities.name: Arrow worm
entities.fact: Arrow worms are glassy, torpedo-shaped predators of the plankton that grab copepods with hooked spines and a venom like that of pufferfish.

entities.name: Nematode
entities.fact: Nematodes are the most abundant animals in deep-sea mud, including the sediments of the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 kilometres down.

entities.name: Sea cucumber
entities.fact: Sea cucumbers breathe through their bottoms and can eject their sticky internal organs at attackers, growing them back within weeks.

entities.name: Sea pig
entities.fact: Sea pigs are pink, pudgy sea cucumbers that walk on tube feet across abyssal plains, often in herds all facing the current, 1,000 to 6,000 metres down.

entities.name: Elpidia
entities.fact: Elpidia are small, stubby sea cucumbers that plough the mud of trench floors in herds, among the most numerous large animals at hadal depths.

entities.name: Headless chicken monster
entities.fact: The headless chicken monster is a translucent pink sea cucumber that swims with a webbed collar and sheds a sticky glowing skin onto anything that touches it.

entities.name: Brittle star
entities.fact: Brittle stars snap off arms to escape predators and grow them back, and they have been seen in large numbers on the floor of the South Sandwich Trench below 6,000 metres.

entities.name: Sea lily
entities.fact: Sea lilies are animals, not plants: feathery filter feeders on a stalk that were common 300 million years ago and today live densely on rocks more than 9,000 metres down in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench.

entities.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
entities.fact: The crown-of-thorns starfish is covered in venomous spines and eats living coral, and outbreaks of it have stripped large areas of the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: Sea urchins walk on hundreds of tube feet and chew with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern, and some species carry venom in their spines.

entities.name: Flower urchin
entities.fact: The flower urchin is the most dangerous sea urchin: its flower-like pincers inject a venom that can cause paralysis and has been blamed for diver deaths.

entities.name: Sponge
entities.fact: Sponges are the simplest animals, with no organs or nerves, yet a carnivorous sponge was dredged from 9,990 metres in the Philippine Trench.

entities.name: Glass sponge
entities.fact: Glass sponges build skeletons of silica glass fibres, and some deep-sea individuals are thought to be more than 10,000 years old.

entities.name: Venus' flower basket
entities.fact: The Venus' flower basket is a lattice-like glass sponge in which a pair of shrimp live trapped for life, which is why dried ones are given as wedding gifts in Japan.

entities.name: Harp sponge
entities.fact: The harp sponge, found 3,300 metres down off California in 2012, is a carnivore: it snags tiny crustaceans on Velcro-like hooks along its harp-shaped branches.

entities.name: Salp
entities.fact: Salps are barrel-shaped, transparent relatives of vertebrates that pump water through their bodies, and can link into chains many metres long.

entities.name: Pyrosome
entities.fact: A pyrosome is a hollow tube of thousands of cloned tunicates that glows blue-green, and some grow longer than a bus.

entities.name: Predatory tunicate
entities.fact: The predatory tunicate is a sea squirt anchored in deep-sea canyons that holds its hood open like a Venus flytrap and snaps it shut on passing animals.

entities.name: Larvacean
entities.fact: Larvaceans are tadpole-shaped, transparent animals that build a disposable mucus 'house' around themselves to filter food, discarding it several times a day.

entities.name: Giant larvacean
entities.fact: The giant larvacean builds a mucus house up to a metre across that filters the deep water and, when abandoned, sinks carbon and microplastics to the seafloor.

entities.name: Doliolid
entities.fact: Doliolids are transparent, barrel-shaped plankton with muscle bands like hoops, and a single founder can bud a chain of hundreds of clones.

entities.name: Chemosynthetic bacteria
entities.fact: Chemosynthetic bacteria make food from the hydrogen sulphide in vent water instead of from sunlight, feeding every animal at a hydrothermal vent.

entities.name: Xenophyophore
entities.fact: Xenophyophores are single cells up to about 10 centimetres across that build mud shells on the seabed, and were found at 10,641 metres in the Mariana Trench.

entities.name: Foraminifera
entities.fact: Foraminifera are single-celled, shell-building organisms, and soft-walled species live in the mud at the very bottom of the Challenger Deep.

entities.name: Giant sea spider
entities.fact: Giant sea spiders of the deep and Antarctic seas can span about 70 centimetres, and pump blood with their guts rather than a strong heart.

entities.name: Vent sea spider
entities.fact: Sericosura sea spiders cluster by the hundred on vent chimneys, sucking up bacterial mats with a tube-like proboscis.

entities.name: Plankton
entities.fact: Plankton means 'wanderer' in Greek: it is every organism, from bacteria to jellyfish, that cannot swim against the current.

entities.name: Zooplankton
entities.fact: Zooplankton are the animal drifters of the sea, from copepods to jellyfish, and each night they rise towards the surface in the largest migration on Earth.

entities.name: Flounder
entities.fact: A flounder starts life swimming upright with an eye on each side, then one eye migrates over the top of its head as it settles to lie flat on the seabed.

entities.name: Halibut
entities.fact: Halibut are the largest flatfish and active hunters, and their name comes from 'holy butt', the flatfish eaten on holy days.

entities.name: Atlantic halibut
entities.fact: The Atlantic halibut can exceed 300 kilograms, the biggest flatfish on record, and heavy fishing has left it scarce across the north-east Atlantic.

entities.name: Pacific halibut
entities.fact: Pacific halibut have been caught weighing more than 200 kilograms, and the fishery is managed jointly by Canada and the United States.

entities.name: Greenland halibut
entities.fact: The Greenland halibut is a flatfish that has partly returned to upright swimming, with its upper eye perched on the top edge of its head.

entities.name: California halibut
entities.fact: The California halibut is a left-eyed flounder, though about 40 per cent of individuals turn out right-eyed, a quirk almost unique among flatfish.

entities.name: Sole
entities.fact: Soles are oval, right-eyed flatfish named after the Latin word for a sandal, which the Romans thought they resembled.

entities.name: Dover sole
entities.fact: The Dover sole, prized by chefs, got its name because the port of Dover supplied more of it to London's markets than anywhere else.

entities.name: Lemon sole
entities.fact: The lemon sole is neither a sole nor lemon-flavoured; it is a small-mouthed right-eyed flounder whose name comes from limande, the French word for dab.

entities.name: Petrale sole
entities.fact: The petrale sole, a right-eyed flounder of the US and Canadian Pacific coast, is one of the most prized flatfish caught there.

entities.name: Yellowfin sole
entities.fact: The yellowfin sole of the Bering Sea supports the largest flatfish fishery in the world by weight.

entities.name: Rex sole
entities.fact: The rex sole is a slender, thin-bodied flatfish of the North Pacific with a very small mouth, usually fried whole on the bone.

entities.name: Moses sole
entities.fact: The Moses sole of the Red Sea oozes a milky, soap-like toxin from its fins that makes sharks spit it out, and the toxin was studied as a shark repellent.

entities.name: Solenette
entities.fact: The solenette is a tiny sole, rarely more than 12 centimetres long, that lies on sandy seabeds around Britain and is thrown back by trawlers.

entities.name: Plaice
entities.fact: The plaice is the flatfish with orange spots, and it can lighten or darken its skin to match the sand it lies on.

entities.name: American plaice
entities.fact: The American plaice, called the long rough dab in Europe, is a cold-water flatfish with a large mouth that lives on both sides of the North Atlantic.

entities.name: Turbot
entities.fact: The turbot is a big, nearly circular, left-eyed flatfish with bony bumps instead of scales, farmed in Spain and prized by chefs.

entities.name: Brill
entities.fact: The brill is a smaller, smoother cousin of the turbot with tiny scales and a frilled front edge to its dorsal fin.

entities.name: Dab
entities.fact: The dab is a small, rough-skinned flatfish, one of the commonest fish on sandy seabeds in the North Sea, and it often buries itself in the sand.

entities.name: Summer flounder
entities.fact: The summer flounder, or fluke, is a sharp-toothed left-eyed flounder that hunts actively and is the favourite flatfish of anglers on the US east coast.

entities.name: European flounder
entities.fact: The European flounder swims far up rivers into fresh water and has even been caught in canals, though it returns to the sea to spawn.

entities.name: Winter flounder
entities.fact: The winter flounder makes antifreeze proteins in its blood to survive winters in New England harbours, and the gene was once tested in tomatoes.

entities.name: Starry flounder
entities.fact: The starry flounder has black-and-orange striped fins and can be left-eyed or right-eyed, with the proportion changing from Japan to California.

entities.name: Peacock flounder
entities.fact: The peacock flounder is covered in blue rings and can match a chequerboard pattern in seconds, and it buries itself in sand with only its eyes showing.

entities.name: Olive flounder
entities.fact: The olive flounder, hirame, is the most farmed fish in South Korea and a prized sushi fish in Japan, served as thin white slices.

entities.name: Tonguefish
entities.fact: Tonguefish are teardrop-shaped flatfish with no pectoral fins and a hooked snout, and one species lives beside pools of molten sulphur at undersea volcanoes.

entities.name: Vent tonguefish
entities.fact: Symphurus thermophilus is a flatfish that lives in crowds at volcanic vents of the western Pacific, resting on crusts of solid sulphur beside pools of the molten stuff.

entities.name: Megrim
entities.fact: The megrim is a thin, big-eyed left-eyed flatfish caught off Cornwall; most of the catch is sold to Spain, where it is called gallo.

entities.name: Witch
entities.fact: The witch is a long, thin, right-eyed flounder of deep muddy seabeds, sold as Torbay sole in Britain and grey sole in North America.

entities.name: Sanddab
entities.fact: Pacific sanddabs are small left-eyed flounders of the US west coast, pan-fried whole and a speciality of Monterey and San Francisco restaurants.

entities.name: Hogchoker
entities.fact: The hogchoker is a small American sole that swims up rivers and got its name because pigs fed on the rough-skinned fish supposedly choked on them.

entities.name: Windowpane flounder
entities.fact: The windowpane flounder is so thin that light passes through its body when it is held up to the sun.

entities.name: Topknot
entities.fact: The topknot is a small, rough-scaled flatfish of rocky shores that clings upside-down beneath ledges rather than lying on sand.

entities.name: Scaldfish
entities.fact: The scaldfish is a small, translucent flatfish of European seas whose loose scales come off so easily that it looks scalded when caught.

entities.name: Arrowtooth flounder
entities.fact: The arrowtooth flounder is the most abundant groundfish in the Gulf of Alaska, but an enzyme turns its flesh to mush when cooked, so it was long discarded.

entities.name: Stingray
entities.fact: Stingrays bury themselves in sand with only their eyes and spiracles showing, and their tail spine is a serrated barb loaded with venom.

entities.name: Southern stingray
entities.fact: Southern stingrays crowd the sandbar at Stingray City in the Cayman Islands, and between feeds lie buried in sand with only their eyes showing.

entities.name: Blue-spotted ribbontail ray
entities.fact: The blue-spotted ribbontail ray has electric-blue spots that warn of its venomous tail spines, and it hides under reef ledges rather than burying in sand.

entities.name: Electric ray
entities.fact: Electric rays bury themselves in sand and stun prey with shocks of up to about 220 volts from kidney-shaped organs in their wings.

entities.name: Numbfish
entities.fact: The Australian numbfish is a flabby electric ray that lies buried in sand and can deliver a strong shock, and it is sometimes stranded alive on beaches.

entities.name: Skate
entities.fact: Skates lay rectangular egg cases called mermaid's purses and rest half-buried in sand or mud with just their eyes exposed.

entities.name: Guitarfish
entities.fact: Guitarfish are half shark and half ray in shape, and spend the day buried in sand with only their eyes and spiracles exposed.

entities.name: Angel shark
entities.fact: The angel shark is a flattened ambush predator that buries itself in sand for days, then snaps up passing fish in a tenth of a second.

entities.name: Stargazer
entities.fact: The stargazer lies buried with only its upturned eyes and mouth above the sand, and some species deliver electric shocks as well as venomous spines.

entities.name: Weever fish
entities.fact: The weever fish buries itself in sand with only its venomous black dorsal fin showing, and is the most common cause of fish stings on British beaches.

entities.name: Sand eel
entities.fact: Sand eels are slim silvery fish that dive headfirst into sand to hide, and puffins and kittiwakes depend on them to feed their chicks.

entities.name: Pacific sand lance
entities.fact: Pacific sand lance spend the night and much of the winter buried in coarse sand, which is why mapping their sand beds matters for salmon and seabirds.

entities.name: Garden eel
entities.fact: Garden eels live in colonies of hundreds, each in its own sand burrow, swaying like grass to catch plankton and sinking out of sight when approached.

entities.name: Snake eel
entities.fact: Snake eels have a hard, pointed tail that they use to burrow backwards into sand, leaving only the head poking out.

entities.name: Ribbon eel
entities.fact: The ribbon eel lives in a burrow in sand or rubble and changes from black to blue to yellow as it turns from juvenile to male to female.

entities.name: Mudskipper
entities.fact: Mudskippers are fish that walk and skip across mud flats, breathe through their skin, and retreat into burrows they dig in the mud.

entities.name: African lungfish
entities.fact: When its pool dries up the African lungfish burrows into mud, wraps itself in a mucus cocoon and breathes air for months, even years, until rain returns.

entities.name: Wrasse
entities.fact: Many wrasses dive into the sand to sleep at night, and most species start life as females and later change into males.

entities.name: Pearly razorfish
entities.fact: The pearly razorfish is a wrasse with a blade-thin head that dives headfirst into sand in an instant to escape, and sleeps buried there.

entities.name: Lizardfish
entities.fact: Lizardfish are toothy ambush hunters that sit on the sand, often with most of the body buried, and dart up to grab passing fish.

entities.name: Flathead
entities.fact: Flatheads lie buried in sand with only their eyes showing, and the dusky flathead is one of Australia's most popular angling fish.

entities.name: Dragonet
entities.fact: Dragonets are small, scaleless fish that bury themselves in sand with only their eyes showing; the male common dragonet has a huge sail-like fin.

entities.name: Cusk-eel
entities.fact: Cusk-eels back tail-first into burrows in sand, and one species was trawled from 8,370 metres in the Puerto Rico Trench, long the record for the deepest fish.

entities.name: Abyssobrotula
entities.fact: Abyssobrotula galatheae is a pale cusk-eel with tiny eyes, recorded from 8,370 metres in the Puerto Rico Trench in 1970, a depth record that stood for decades.

entities.name: Stonefish
entities.fact: The stonefish is the most venomous fish known, with 13 dorsal spines, and lies half-buried in sand looking exactly like an encrusted rock.

entities.name: Pacific sandfish
entities.fact: The Pacific sandfish buries itself in sand with just its upturned mouth exposed, and is a key prey of seabirds and salmon in Alaska.

entities.name: Swamp eel
entities.fact: The Asian swamp eel breathes air, burrows into mud when ponds dry out, and has become an invader of Florida and Georgia wetlands.

entities.name: Weather loach
entities.fact: The weather loach burrows into mud to survive drought and gets its name from becoming restless when the air pressure drops before a storm.

entities.name: Anglerfish
entities.fact: The female deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure of bacteria in front of her mouth, and in some species the tiny male fuses onto her body for life.

entities.name: Humpback anglerfish
entities.fact: The humpback anglerfish is the classic toothy black angler that appears in Finding Nemo, and the male is about a tenth the length of the female.

entities.name: Footballfish
entities.fact: Footballfish are round-bodied deep-sea anglers; several have washed up on California beaches, a rare sight of a fish from about 1,000 metres down.

entities.name: Blobfish
entities.fact: The blobfish looks normal at its home depth of 600 to 1,200 metres; its famous droopy face is what happens when its jelly-like flesh is hauled to the surface.

entities.name: Viperfish
entities.fact: The viperfish's fangs are so long they do not fit inside its mouth, and it has been recorded deeper than 4,000 metres.

entities.name: Gulper eel
entities.fact: The gulper eel's mouth is bigger than the rest of its body, and it can balloon out like a pelican's pouch to swallow prey larger than itself.

entities.name: Lanternfish
entities.fact: Lanternfish may make up more than half of all deep-sea fish by weight, and their nightly rise towards the surface is the largest animal migration on Earth.

entities.name: Fangtooth
entities.fact: The fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish relative to its body size, so big that it has sockets in its skull for them to fit into.

entities.name: Goblin shark
entities.fact: The goblin shark's jaws shoot forward out of its face to snatch prey, and its pink skin and blade-like snout make it look like a living fossil.

entities.name: Barreleye
entities.fact: The barreleye has a transparent dome over its head and tubular green eyes that rotate inside it to look up through its own skull.

entities.name: Dragonfish
entities.fact: Deep-sea dragonfish have transparent teeth, a glowing chin barbel, and jaws that can open past 100 degrees.

entities.name: Stoplight loosejaw
entities.fact: The stoplight loosejaw shines a red searchlight that most deep-sea animals cannot see, and has a jaw with no floor so it can snap shut faster.

entities.name: Hatchetfish
entities.fact: Hatchetfish are silver, blade-thin fish with photophores on their bellies that match the faint light from above, making them invisible from below.

entities.name: Oarfish
entities.fact: The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish, reaching about 8 metres, and its rare strandings probably inspired sea-serpent legends.

entities.name: Frilled shark
entities.fact: The frilled shark has an eel-like body, about 300 needle-like teeth in 25 rows and a pregnancy thought to last up to three and a half years.

entities.name: Snailfish
entities.fact: Snailfish are the deepest-living fish known: one was filmed at 8,336 metres in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench in 2022.

entities.name: Mariana snailfish
entities.fact: The Mariana snailfish, named in 2017, has been collected from nearly 8,000 metres and has a see-through pink body with no scales.

entities.name: Ethereal snailfish
entities.fact: The ethereal snailfish was filmed at 8,145 metres in the Mariana Trench in 2014, a wispy, nearly transparent fish that has never been caught.

entities.name: Kermadec snailfish
entities.fact: The Kermadec snailfish lives only in the Kermadec Trench off New Zealand, where it has been filmed feeding in groups about 7,500 metres down.

entities.name: Grenadier
entities.fact: Grenadiers, or rattails, are the commonest fish on the deep seabed, with big heads and whip-like tails, and have been seen about 7,000 metres down.

entities.name: Abyssal grenadier
entities.fact: The abyssal grenadier roams abyssal plains worldwide between about 2,000 and 5,000 metres, following its nose to carcasses that sink from above.

entities.name: Cookiecutter shark
entities.fact: The cookiecutter shark glows on its belly and bites neat round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna and even the rubber of submarines.

entities.name: Megamouth shark
entities.fact: The megamouth shark was unknown to science until 1976, when one swallowed a US Navy sea anchor off Hawaii; fewer than 300 have been seen since.

entities.name: Coelacanth
entities.fact: The coelacanth was thought extinct for 66 million years until a fisherman landed one off South Africa in 1938; it lives in caves around 200 metres down.

entities.name: Black swallower
entities.fact: The black swallower can gulp down fish more than twice its own length, stretching its stomach so far that it sometimes bursts.

entities.name: Tripod fish
entities.fact: The tripod fish stands motionless on the abyssal floor on three stiff fin rays up to a metre long, facing the current with its mouth open.

entities.name: Hagfish
entities.fact: A hagfish can turn a bucket of water into slime in seconds, ties itself in a knot to wipe it off, and feeds on carcasses thousands of metres down.

entities.name: Orange roughy
entities.fact: The orange roughy lives at 500 to 1,500 metres, does not breed until its twenties and can live for about 150 years, which is why it was so easily overfished.

entities.name: Patagonian toothfish
entities.fact: The Patagonian toothfish was renamed 'Chilean sea bass' by a fish wholesaler in 1977 to sell it, and lives down to about 3,800 metres.

entities.name: Greenland shark
entities.fact: The Greenland shark can live for about 400 years, the longest of any vertebrate, and its flesh is poisonous unless fermented into Icelandic hákarl.

entities.name: Sixgill shark
entities.fact: The bluntnose sixgill shark has six gill slits instead of five, grows to about 5 metres and spends the day down to about 2,500 metres.

entities.name: Lancetfish
entities.fact: The lancetfish is a 2-metre deep-sea predator with a huge sail fin and fangs, and its watery flesh is so flabby that it is rarely eaten.

entities.name: Bristlemouth
entities.fact: Bristlemouths are tiny, glowing deep-sea fish that may number in the hundreds of trillions, making them the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.

entities.name: Telescopefish
entities.fact: The telescopefish has forward-pointing tubular eyes like a pair of binoculars and can swallow prey longer than itself.

entities.name: Sabertooth fish
entities.fact: Sabertooth fish are small deep-sea hunters with upward-looking eyes and fangs that stick out past the jaw.

entities.name: Snipe eel
entities.fact: The snipe eel has a body like a ribbon and thin, outward-curving jaws like a bird's beak that cannot close, which it uses to snag shrimp by their antennae.

entities.name: Portuguese dogfish
entities.fact: The Portuguese dogfish is the deepest-living shark known, recorded at about 3,675 metres.

entities.name: Black scabbardfish
entities.fact: The black scabbardfish is a jet-black, eel-like deep-sea fish with fangs, hauled up from about 1,000 metres on long lines off Madeira, where it is served with banana.

entities.name: Pacific sleeper shark
entities.fact: The Pacific sleeper shark is a sluggish giant up to about 4.5 metres long that lives down to about 2,000 metres in the North Pacific.

entities.name: Blue antimora
entities.fact: The blue antimora is a deep-sea cod relative with a violet sheen, common on continental slopes from about 800 to 3,000 metres.

entities.name: Deep-sea lizardfish
entities.fact: The deep-sea lizardfish is a toothy ambush predator of abyssal plains between about 1,000 and 3,500 metres, and is both male and female at once.

entities.name: Halosaur
entities.fact: Halosaurs are long-tailed, eel-like fish of the deep seabed, swimming slowly over abyssal mud below 1,000 metres with a snout that overhangs the mouth.

entities.name: Flabby whalefish
entities.fact: Flabby whalefish live below about 1,500 metres and look so different from their own larvae and males that the three were once classed as separate families.

entities.name: Eelpout
entities.fact: Eelpouts are blunt-headed, eel-shaped fish of cold seas; some live at hydrothermal vents and others on abyssal plains below 4,000 metres.

entities.name: Pink vent fish
entities.fact: The pink vent fish is an eelpout found only at East Pacific vents, where it lies among the tube worms and eats limpets and amphipods.

entities.name: Bony-eared assfish
entities.fact: The bony-eared assfish is a cusk-eel from 1,000 to 4,400 metres with the smallest brain for its body size of any known vertebrate, and an unfortunate name.

entities.name: Flashlight fish
entities.fact: Flashlight fish have bean-shaped pouches of glowing bacteria under each eye, which they blink by rolling or shuttering the organ.

entities.name: Lanternshark
entities.fact: Lanternsharks are small, deep-water sharks with glowing bellies, and the velvet belly lanternshark has light-up spines on its back to warn off predators.

entities.name: Kitefin shark
entities.fact: The kitefin shark, up to about 1.8 metres long, was confirmed in 2021 to be the largest glowing vertebrate known.

entities.name: Midshipman
entities.fact: The plainfin midshipman has rows of photophores like the buttons on a naval uniform, and the humming of the males keeps houseboat residents awake in Sausalito.

entities.name: Pinecone fish
entities.fact: The pinecone fish is armoured in big plated scales and carries glowing bacteria in two light organs on its lower jaw to lure prey at night.

entities.name: Ponyfish
entities.fact: Ponyfish keep glowing bacteria in a ring-shaped organ around the throat and shine the light out through transparent windows in their bellies.

entities.name: Transparent goby
entities.fact: The transparent goby is a see-through, finger-length fish of European coasts that lives only a year and is eaten by the plateful as whitebait in Italy and Spain.

entities.name: Crystal goby
entities.fact: The crystal goby is an almost invisible, glass-bodied fish that lives in open water off European coasts rather than on the seabed like most gobies.

entities.name: Glass eel
entities.fact: Young eels arriving at European and American coasts after drifting from the Sargasso Sea are called glass eels because their bodies are completely transparent.

entities.name: Leptocephalus
entities.fact: The leptocephalus is the leaf-shaped, see-through larva of eels, tarpon and bonefish, which drifts in the current for months before changing shape.

entities.name: Pufferfish
entities.fact: Pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin, a poison with no antidote that is about 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide, yet fugu is a Japanese delicacy.

entities.name: Porcupinefish
entities.fact: The porcupinefish inflates into a spiky ball when threatened, and its skin and organs carry tetrodotoxin, so it is poisonous to eat.

entities.name: Lionfish
entities.fact: Lionfish have 18 venomous spines and, released from aquariums, have invaded the Caribbean and western Atlantic, where they have no natural predators.

entities.name: Scorpionfish
entities.fact: Scorpionfish are camouflaged ambush hunters with venomous fin spines, and the family includes the lionfish and the stonefish.

entities.name: Rabbitfish
entities.fact: Rabbitfish are harmless-looking reef grazers with venomous spines in their fins that cause an agonising sting if handled.

entities.name: Striped eel catfish
entities.fact: Juvenile striped eel catfish swarm in tight balls on reefs, and each one carries venomous spines that have caused rare human deaths.

entities.name: Boxfish
entities.fact: Boxfish are encased in a rigid bony box and, when stressed, release a poisonous mucus that can kill every other fish in an aquarium.

entities.name: Spiny dogfish
entities.fact: The spiny dogfish has a mildly venomous spine in front of each dorsal fin, and was long sold in British fish and chip shops as rock salmon.

entities.name: Port Jackson shark
entities.fact: The Port Jackson shark has a venomous spine in front of each dorsal fin and lays spiral egg cases that it wedges into rock crevices.

entities.name: Spotted ratfish
entities.fact: The spotted ratfish, a chimaera with rabbit-like teeth and a rat-like tail, carries a venomous spine on its back.

entities.name: Sea snake
entities.fact: Sea snakes are among the most venomous snakes on Earth, with paddle-shaped tails, and most give birth to live young at sea without ever coming ashore.

entities.name: Yellow-bellied sea snake
entities.fact: The yellow-bellied sea snake is the most widespread snake on Earth, drifting across the tropical Pacific and Indian Oceans and drinking rain from the sea surface.

entities.name: Belcher's sea snake
entities.fact: Belcher's sea snake is often called the most venomous snake in the world, though it is so docile that bites are extremely rare.

entities.name: Whale
entities.fact: Baleen whales have no teeth; they gulp or skim water and strain out krill and small fish through fringed plates of keratin in their jaws.

entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: A blue whale, the largest animal ever to live, can eat several tonnes of krill a day and very little else.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Humpback whales blow spiralling curtains of bubbles to herd krill and small fish into a tight ball before lunging through it with mouths open.

entities.name: Fin whale
entities.fact: The fin whale, second only to the blue whale in size, lunges at krill swarms at speed and has a lower jaw that is white on the right side and dark on the left.

entities.name: Minke whale
entities.fact: The minke whale is the smallest of the rorquals and feeds on krill and small schooling fish; it is still hunted by Norway, Iceland and Japan.

entities.name: Antarctic minke whale
entities.fact: The Antarctic minke whale feeds almost entirely on krill under and around the pack ice and was the main target of Japan's Antarctic whaling.

entities.name: Sei whale
entities.fact: The sei whale skims the surface for copepods and krill and is one of the fastest great whales, capable of about 50 kilometres per hour in bursts.

entities.name: Southern right whale
entities.fact: The southern right whale skims swarms of krill and copepods through its baleen, and was named 'right' because whalers found it the right whale to kill.

entities.name: Bowhead whale
entities.fact: The bowhead whale filters krill and copepods through the longest baleen of any whale, and can live for more than 200 years.

entities.name: Bryde's whale
